name: Hanoi
tagline: Lakeside temples, French boulevards and old-quarter bustle.
whenBlurb: Autumn, September to November, is the city at its finest: warm sun, dry air, mild light. Skip the wet summer heat and grey, damp winter.

ourTake.lede: Give Hanoi more time than people assume, its pleasures are slow and best taken on foot, ideally at dawn when the lakes belong to tai chi practitioners and the pho stalls are at their sharpest. Skip the packaged water-puppet show and the frantic Old Quarter shopping; the real city is in the crumbling French villas of Ba Dinh, the egg-coffee balconies, and a long lunch of bun cha where Obama once sat. The weather makes or breaks a trip: come in autumn (October–November) for dry, cool days, and avoid the grey drizzle of February and March.
ourTake.comeIf: You want old-quarter atmosphere, brilliant street food and Halong Bay a short drive away.
ourTake.skipIf: You want beaches and resorts; Hanoi is a city of culture, not a place to lie still.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Capella Hanoi
items.area: French Quarter / near the Opera House (Hoan Kiem)
items.description: Bill Bensley's 1920s opera fantasy, 47 rooms, each a jewel-box, and the finest address in the city.

items.name: Sofitel Legend Metropole Hanoi
credentials: Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star (2025, fifth consecutive year)
Condé Nast Traveler Gold List 2025 (only hotel in Vietnam)
items.description: The city's grande dame since 1901, colonial white-and-green, and the address every visitor of consequence has passed through.

items.name: InterContinental Hanoi Westlake
items.description: Over-water pavilions on stilts above West Lake, a resort calm rare this close to the centre.

items.name: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi
items.area: Nam Tu Liem / Convention district (west Hanoi)
items.description: Carlos Zapata's dragon-inspired curve, the capital's grand modern house, chosen for heads of state.

items.name: Meliá Hanoi
items.description: A dependable, well-placed international tower in the heart of the city.

items.name: Apricot Hotel
items.description: An art-filled boutique house facing Hoan Kiem Lake, Vietnamese paintings on every wall.

items.name: Peridot Grand Luxury Boutique Hotel
items.description: A polished, urbane boutique tower in the thick of the Old Quarter.

items.name: The Old Quarter, the 36 guild streets
items.description: A thousand years of commerce still hums through this warren north of the lake, where each lane once served a single trade, Hang Bac for silver, Hang Ma for votive paper, Hang Dao for silk. Best walked slowly with a private guide who can read the layers a map cannot.

items.name: A cyclo ride through the old lanes
items.description: The gentlest way to take in the crush of the 36 streets, reclined in a pedalled cyclo while the city flows around you, unhurried and eye-level with the shophouses. An easy, charming loop for elders and children alike before the walking begins.

items.name: Hoan Kiem Lake
items.description: The green heart of Hanoi and the city's favourite gathering place, its still water wrapped in willows and the legend of the returned sword. A dawn circuit past the red Turtle Tower, when locals practise tai chi, is one of the quietest luxuries the city offers.

items.name: Ngoc Son Temple & The Huc Bridge
items.description: A small island temple honouring the general Tran Hung Dao, reached across the vivid vermilion arc of The Huc Bridge. The postcard image of Hanoi, and a serene ten-minute pause in the middle of the old city.

items.name: Temple of Literature
items.description: Vietnam's first university, founded in 1070, a series of tranquil walled courtyards, lotus ponds and stelae carried on the backs of stone tortoises. The most composed and contemplative site in the city, and one that resonates with multi-generation families who prize learning.

items.name: Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum & Ba Dinh Square
items.description: The solemn granite mausoleum on the vast ceremonial square where independence was declared in 1945, its changing of the guard a study in precision. A window into the nation's founding story, go early, and dress modestly.

items.name: One Pillar Pagoda
items.description: A tiny wooden shrine built in 1049 to resemble a lotus rising on a single stone stem from its pond, tucked within the Ho Chi Minh complex. Small in scale but singular in form, worth the short walk from the mausoleum.

items.name: Presidential Palace & Ho Chi Minh's stilt house
items.description: The mustard-yellow French colonial palace with its formal gardens, and behind it the modest teak stilt house where Ho Chi Minh chose to live instead. The contrast between grandeur and simplicity is the whole point.

items.name: Ho Chi Minh Museum
items.description: A striking modernist white building beside the mausoleum, its exhibits tracing the life of the leader and the century that shaped modern Vietnam. A cool, orderly stop that completes the Ba Dinh circuit.

items.name: Imperial Citadel of Thang Long
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Central Sector of the Imperial Citadel of Thang Long
items.description: A thousand years of Vietnamese power layered in one place, Ly dynasty palace foundations, colonial gates and the underground command bunker of the American war, all in a single vast enclosure. The archaeological dig alone rewards a private, well-guided morning.

items.name: The Old French Quarter
items.description: Wide tree-lined boulevards, ochre villas and grand hotels laid out during the colonial decades, a world away from the tangle of the Old Quarter. Best explored on foot or by private car, ending with tea at the Metropole where egg coffee was born.

items.name: Hanoi Opera House
items.description: A 1911 belle-epoque theatre modelled on the Palais Garnier in Paris, all marble stairs and gilt, still staging opera, ballet and Vietnamese folk concerts. Attend a performance, or simply admire the finest colonial facade in the city.

items.name: St Joseph's Cathedral
items.description: A weathered neo-Gothic cathedral from 1886, its twin towers echoing Notre-Dame, presiding over a lively square ringed with cafes. The lanes around it, Nha Tho and Nha Chung, are among the best in the city for a slow coffee and boutique browsing.

items.name: Vietnam Museum of Ethnology
items.description: The finest museum in Hanoi, a thoughtful, superbly labelled survey of Vietnam's 54 ethnic groups, with full-scale traditional houses reconstructed in the garden. Genuinely engaging for children and the most rewarding cultural stop in the city.

items.name: Vietnamese Women's Museum
items.description: A moving, beautifully curated museum on women in Vietnamese life, marriage, motherhood, war and the street vendors who still carry the city on shoulder poles. Compact, powerful and a short walk south of the lake.

items.name: Vietnam National Fine Arts Museum
items.description: Set in an elegant three-storey colonial building, a well-chosen collection running from ancient Buddhist sculpture and lacquer to modern silk painting. Quiet, uncrowded and close to the Temple of Literature.

items.name: Hoa Lo Prison
items.description: The remnant of the French colonial prison, later the wartime 'Hanoi Hilton', with unflinching exhibits on both eras. Sobering and well-presented, a serious counterweight to the city's gentler sights.

items.name: Train Street
items.description: A famously narrow residential lane where a working train passes within arm's reach of the trackside cafes. Access has been repeatedly restricted for safety and opens and closes without notice, go only with a local guide who knows the day's rules.

items.name: West Lake (Ho Tay)
items.description: The city's largest lake, ringed by 17 km of quieter, leafier streets, lakeside villas and the best independent dining in Hanoi. A calm base for a slower stay, with sunset the moment to be on the water's edge.

items.name: Tran Quoc Pagoda
items.description: The oldest Buddhist temple in Hanoi, its red brick stupa rising from a slender causeway into West Lake, dating in origin to the 6th century. Loveliest in late afternoon when the light catches the water and incense drifts from the shrine.

items.name: Quan Thanh Temple
items.description: A serene 11th-century Taoist temple beside West Lake, guarded by a nearly four-metre bronze statue cast in the 17th century. An easy, atmospheric pairing with Tran Quoc just along the shore.

items.name: Dong Xuan Market
items.description: Hanoi's largest covered market, a French-built hall of narrow aisles selling everything from silk and spices to household goods. Chaotic and colourful, a photographer's paradise and a plunge into the working city.

items.name: Thang Long Water Puppet Theatre
items.description: A thousand-year-old northern art form performed on a pool of water, lacquered puppets dancing to live traditional music and folk tales of rice farming and dragons. Short, delightful and a sure hit across three generations.

items.name: Egg coffee (ca phe trung)
items.description: Hanoi's signature indulgence, whipped egg yolk beaten into a rich sweet cream over strong coffee, invented here in 1946. Cafe Giang, run by the inventor's family, is the original; a hidden upstairs table watching the street is part of the ritual.

items.name: Old Quarter street-food trail
items.description: Hanoi is a world capital of street food, pho, bun cha over charcoal, banh cuon, egg coffee, each often mastered by a single family stall. A private evening food guide navigates the crowds, the hygiene and the vegetarian options with ease.

items.name: Bat Trang ceramics village
items.description: A 15th-century pottery village 15 km from the centre, its lanes lined with kilns and workshops where you can throw and paint your own piece to be fired and shipped home. A hands-on half-day that delights families and design lovers alike.

items.name: Long Bien Bridge
items.description: The great 1902 Eiffel-era iron bridge across the Red River, scarred by war and still carrying trains and cyclists over the water and the banana fields below. A quietly poignant walk at golden hour, away from the tour crowds.

items.name: Hang Ma & the craft lanes at festival time
items.description: The lane of votive paper and decorations erupts into colour before Tet and the Mid-Autumn Festival, lanterns and offerings spilling across the street. Timed right, it is one of the most joyous corners of the city.

items.name: Ba Dinh & the diplomatic quarter by car
items.description: Beyond the mausoleum, the leafy avenues of embassies, ministries and grand villas make a graceful private drive between the citadel and West Lake. A restful way to link the morning's monuments.

items.name: Ha Long Bay overnight cruise
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Ha Long Bay
items.description: Nearly 2,000 limestone karsts rising from jade water, best seen from the balcony cabin of a small luxury junk on an overnight sailing, sunset on the sundeck, kayaking hidden lagoons, dawn tai chi. The single most romantic escape from Hanoi, roughly a 2.5-hour transfer away.

items.name: Lan Ha Bay cruise
items.description: The quieter, less-visited neighbour of Ha Long off Cat Ba Island, the same soaring karsts and secret beaches, with a fraction of the boats. The connoisseur's choice for an overnight cruise, reached in about three hours.

items.name: Ninh Binh & Trang An
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Trang An Landscape Complex
items.description: 'Ha Long Bay on land', rowed in a sampan through flooded caves between towering karsts and rice paddies, past ancient temples and the old capital of Hoa Lu. Utterly cinematic, doable as a long day trip or, better, an overnight from Hanoi.

items.name: Tam Coc & Mua Cave
items.description: The Tam Coc river boats drift through three caves and golden paddies, while a climb of some 500 steps to the Mua Cave viewpoint delivers the definitive panorama over the karst valley. The signature photograph of northern Vietnam.

items.name: Bai Dinh Pagoda
items.description: The largest Buddhist temple complex in Vietnam, a vast modern hillside of halls, a corridor lined with 500 stone arhats and the tallest bronze Buddha in Southeast Asia. Often paired with Trang An on the same Ninh Binh circuit.

items.name: Perfume Pagoda
items.description: A revered pilgrimage of shrines set in a limestone massif, reached by a rowed boat along the Yen stream and then a cable car or hike to the sacred Huong Tich grotto. Loveliest and busiest during the spring festival; serene the rest of the year, about two hours from the city.

items.name: Duong Lam ancient village
items.description: A cluster of hamlets 50 km from Hanoi where 300- to 400-year-old laterite houses, communal halls and banyan-shaded gates preserve the northern delta village of another century. The first village in Vietnam granted national heritage status, a gentle, authentic day in the countryside.

items.name: Mai Chau valley
items.description: A wide green valley of rice terraces and White Thai stilt-house villages, ideal for cycling between hamlets and an overnight stay among the ethnic-minority communities. A soft, scenic introduction to the northern highlands, about four hours out.

items.name: Sapa & Fansipan
items.description: The terraced mountains of the far north, home to Hmong and Dao communities, with Fansipan, the 'Roof of Indochina' at 3,143 m, reached by a modern cable car to summit shrines. A five-hour journey best given two or three days, ideally with a private guide and mountain lodge.

items.name: Ancient House at 87 Ma May
items.description: A restored 19th-century merchant's tube-house open to visitors, its dim rooms and inner courtyard showing exactly how the Old Quarter's traders lived and worked. A five-minute masterclass in vernacular architecture in the heart of the lanes.

items.name: Bach Ma Temple
items.description: The oldest temple in the Old Quarter, dedicated to the white horse spirit said to have guided the founding of the citadel, hushed and incense-dark amid the market bustle. A quiet detour most visitors miss.

items.name: Vietnam Military History Museum
items.description: The nation's flagship military museum, reopened in 2024 in a vast new campus, tracing centuries of resistance through aircraft, tanks and a soaring victory tower. Sweeping, modern and thorough for those drawn to the war years.

items.name: Hanoi cooking class
items.description: A guided morning at the market followed by a private hands-on class in pho, fresh spring rolls and bun cha, with vegetarian menus arranged in advance. A hands-on souvenir the whole family carries home.

items.name: Ceramic Mosaic Mural along the Red River dyke
items.description: A record-holding ceramic mural running several kilometres along the dyke road, telling Vietnamese history in tiny tiles. A colourful, offbeat stop en route to the Long Bien Bridge or Bat Trang.

items.name: Tay Ho lakeside dining & sunset drinks
items.description: West Lake's shore holds Hanoi's most relaxed fine dining and rooftop bars, the water turning gold as the city lights come up. The natural place for a slow, elegant evening away from Old Quarter's clamour.

items.name: Hibana by Koki
items.description: An intimate teppanyaki counter inside Capella, Japanese precision and premium produce, one of the hardest seats in town.

items.name: Gia
items.area: Van Mieu / Dong Da (near the Temple of Literature)
items.description: A modern love letter to Northern Vietnamese heritage, in an Indochine house opposite the Temple of Literature.

items.name: Tầm Vị
items.description: Northern Vietnamese home cooking, kept exact and unhurried, the food a Hanoi grandmother would cook, raised to a star.

items.name: ONVIT
items.area: Yen Hoa / Cau Giay (Grand Plaza Hanoi)
items.description: Korean fine dining told through Vietnam's finest ingredients, the country's first starred Korean kitchen.

items.name: Lamai Garden
items.description: Farm-to-table plant-based cooking with more than half its herbs and vegetables grown on site, a rare green star.

items.name: Chả Cá Thăng Long
items.description: Hanoi's signature turmeric-and-dill fish, sizzled at your table over a charcoal brazier, a single, perfect dish.

items.name: Hà Thành Mansion
items.description: Classic Hanoi cooking in a handsome heritage setting, the old recipes, comfortably staged.

items.name: Ưu Đàm Chay
items.description: Refined vegetarian Vietnamese cooking in a calm, tea-house setting, meat-free without compromise.

items.name: 1946 Cửa Bắc
items.description: Authentic regional Vietnamese dishes in an old villa, quiet, generous, of another era.

items.name: Bún Chả Ta
items.description: Grilled pork and rice noodles in smoky broth, Hanoi's defining lunch, done properly.

items.name: Phở Bò Lâm
items.description: A bowl of beef phở with real conviction, the broth that makes the pilgrimage worth it.

items.name: Miến Lươn Đông Thịnh
items.description: Crisp eel and glass noodles, a Hanoi speciality guarded by a single family.

items.name: Mậu Dịch Số 37
items.description: Vietnamese comfort food in a nostalgic subsidy-era canteen, a warm plate of the country's recent past.

items.name: Bún Chả Hương Liên
items.description: The bún chả joint where Obama and Anthony Bourdain shared a plate and a beer, since immortalised.

items.name: Phở Gia Truyền Bát Đàn
items.description: The queue-out-the-door phở the locals line up for at dawn, a legendary bowl and no ceremony.

items.name: Bamboo Bar, Sofitel Legend Metropole
credentials: Inside the Metropole, a MICHELIN One-Key, Forbes Five-Star landmark hotel
items.description: A poolside Indochine bar in the city's grande dame, a rediscovered wartime air-raid shelter lies just beneath it.

items.name: Workshop14
items.description: The city's most exciting new bar, local ingredients, serious technique, and a place on Asia's list within months of opening.

items.name: The Hudson Rooms
items.description: A dazzling bar inside the Three-Key Capella, 1920s glamour and cocktails to match the setting.

items.name: The Haflington
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2024 (No. 50), Vietnam's first top-50 bar
items.description: A cocktail bar staged like a night in a European museum, the first Vietnamese bar ever to break Asia's top 50.

items.name: Nê Cocktail Bar
items.description: The bar that put Hanoi on the map, birthplace of the celebrated 'Phở' cocktail, distilling the city into a glass.

items.name: Top of Hanoi, Lotte Hotel
credentials: Hanoi's highest rooftop bar, atop the 65-storey Lotte Tower
items.description: An open-air perch on the 67th floor of the Lotte Tower, the highest, widest view over the whole city.

plan.heading: 3 days in Hanoi, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Settle into the Sofitel Legend Metropole, then walk the shaded lanes around Hoan Kiem Lake to the Ngoc Son Temple before the day warms.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Cross into the Old Quarter's guild streets, Hang Bac, Hang Gai, for lacquer and raw silk, ending with tea at a rooftop above St. Joseph's Cathedral.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Gia by chef Sam Tran, whose tasting menu reads Hanoi through the seasons; a quiet nightcap back at the Metropole's Bamboo Bar.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Early visit to the Temple of Literature, then the Ho Chi Minh complex and the stilt house while the grounds are still cool.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Coffee and lacquerware at the Vietnamese Women's Museum, then a slow afternoon at the Sofitel spa.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Bun cha done properly at a family house, then Michelin-listed T.U.N.G by Hoang Tung for a modern Vietnamese tasting.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Private car to Bat Trang, the eight-century pottery village, to watch the wheels and choose a few pieces to ship home.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Return for a leisurely lunch, then the Thang Long water puppet theatre, an old art, done with real care.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: A farewell dinner at La Verticale in a French villa, chef Didier Corlou's take on Vietnamese spice.

items.name: Old Quarter (Hoan Kiem)
items.description: The dense, motorbike-loud heart of the city, best for first-timers who want to walk everywhere and don't mind noise.

items.name: French Quarter
items.description: Wide boulevards, the opera house and the grand old Metropole; suits travellers wanting quiet, space and the classic colonial hotels.

items.name: Tay Ho (West Lake)
items.description: Leafy, lakeside and expat-favoured, with the best cafes and slower mornings, ideal for a longer, more residential stay.

events.name: Tet (Vietnamese Lunar New Year)
events.note: The country's biggest holiday; Hanoi empties of traffic and fills with kumquat trees and peach blossom, though many shops close for several days.

events.name: Dong Da Festival
events.note: Held on the 5th day of the lunar new year at Dong Da mound, it commemorates Emperor Quang Trung's 1789 rout of the invading Qing army.

events.name: Perfume Pagoda Festival
events.note: A months-long pilgrimage southwest of Hanoi where over a million make the boat-and-climb journey to the sacred cave temple.

events.name: Mid-Autumn Festival
events.note: A children's festival that turns Hang Ma street and the Old Quarter into a lantern market with lion dances and mooncakes.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Base yourself around Hoan Kiem Lake or West Lake for calm; dress lightly but cover shoulders and knees at the Temple of Literature and pagodas, and note that traffic crossing is done slowly and steadily rather than by waiting for a gap.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Noi Bai International (HAN); a pre-arranged private car with a fast-track greeter clears you through immigration and covers the 45-minute run into the Old Quarter or West Lake.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: Keep a private car and driver on call; the Old Quarter itself is best on foot, as its lanes are too narrow and chaotic for a vehicle.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: eSIM (Viettel or Vinaphone) activates on landing and is the cleanest option; hotel and restaurant wifi is fast and widespread.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: Vietnamese dong (VND); cards are accepted at hotels and finer restaurants but carry cash for markets and small vendors, and tipping is modest and appreciated rather than expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: October to April is dry, cool and clear, October is the pick. Skip June to August: 35C-plus with humidity over 80% makes it feel like 40, and September brings the wettest, typhoon-remnant rain.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: Direct from Delhi in about 4h30m on Air India, Vietnam Airlines, IndiGo or Vietjet into Noi Bai (HAN); from Mumbai and Bengaluru it is usually one stop via a Vietnamese or Southeast Asian hub. Vietnam Airlines flies it well in business; the DEL service is an overnight departure, so plan to arrive and rest rather than schedule the morning.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No mandatory vaccinations for arrivals from India; hepatitis A, typhoid and routine boosters are sensible. Vietnam is very safe for travellers, petty theft in the Old Quarter is the main watch-out. Drink bottled or filtered water only; tap is not potable.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian is easy and Buddhist 'chay' cooking is a genuine cuisine here, so pure-veg and near-Jain (no onion/garlic on request) is workable at temple-style restaurants. Indian food is available but limited; Namaste Hanoi and Foodshop 45 are the reliable names for a proper Indian meal.
